What 'dark matter' itself is, is unknown.

The name is just a placeholder to signify some significant source of gravity that we can not see with our technology or visibly.

Basically, galaxies/stars act differently in terms of their orbit and such than our current understanding of gravity says they should, in that they frequently act like more matter than we can detect should be there. "Dark matter" is just a term for whatever fills this "matter deficit." It's basically stuff that we don't know what it is, but we're pretty sure something is there.

Dark matter interacts gravitationally. This leaves a whole slew of indirect ways to measure it. There has also already supposedly been a confirmation of a technique for directly detecting it, but that's under scrutiny and another experiment is currently underway to refute (or confirm) their findings. A more accurate analogy would be if there was this area where there seemed to be nothing but yet you could touch it and thus measure it, things would bounce off of it, and so on. You just couldn't see it. And so you label it simply invisible object. The fact it's invisible certainly wouldn't mean it doesn't exist!

The fact that things don't necessarily interact with 'normal' matter is not exactly new. For instance neutrinos. Neutrinos have now been directly detected but were first 'theoretically discovered' (which is just a fancy way of saying hypothesized) in the 1930s by Wolfgang Pauli. Pauli expected them to be so tiny that we might never discover them, and indeed it wasn't until 1956 that a supposed direct detection was published and then 1995 that a Nobel Prize was given as an acknowledgement for the correctness of that detection. Right now there are hundreds of billions of neutrinos zooming in and out of your body in all different directions. Doesn't even tickle, does it?

So the big thing about dark matter is that it definitely does interact gravitationally. This is why the leading hypothesis for the cause of dark matter are WIMPs or weakly interacting massive particles. These are big boys, by particle standards, that don't interact in the normal ways (electromagnet, strong/weak nuclear) but only gravitationally. But because they do interact gravitationally there's still clumping, they still attract other objects, and so on. That's how we were able to detect them in this galaxy. In order to rotate around something (along with maintaining a certain speed of rotation) the entity (be it a planet, galaxy, or whatever) you're rotating about needs a certain mass. The stars in this system are able to rotating at a rate that indicates there is far more mass in this galaxy than we can detect. And there is no lensing or other things indicating invisible baryonic matter, like perhaps a dim star or black hole, and so it lends itself to being dark matter.
